newsitem.title: USA: Storm heads into New England after hitting New York.
newsitem.headline: Storm heads into New England after hitting New York.

text.p: A storm that drenched the New York City area moved into New England on Sunday after causing at least one death and leaving more than 100,000 homes without electricity, officials said.
A 12-year-old boy in Babylon, Long Island, died when a tree uprooted by the storm fell on him, and about 400 people were evacuated on Saturday as a precaution against flooding, officials said.
The storm on Saturday dumped more than eight inches (20 cm) of rain in portions of the New York City-New Jersey metropolitan area.
"The storm actually developed on top of us. It came from nowhere. It actually formed right on top of New York City," said Joe Goudsward, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service.

As of 6 a.m. (1000 GMT) on Sunday, the National Weather Service had cancelled its flood warning for Long Island. "It has been determined that tides are only running about 1 1/2 feet (0.5 meters) above normal ... considerably less than had been expected," it said in a statement.
But it did issue a flood warning for north central Connecticut, where more than three inches (7.6 cm) of rain had fallen by early Sunday across Hartford and Tolland counties.
A flood watch was also in effect for all of Rhode Island, Massachusetts, and southern New Hampshire, as four to six inches of rain (10-15 cm) were expected on Sunday.
"This will certainly cause considerable street flooding and flooding in poor drainage areas as storm drains become clogged with leaves," the agency said.

The rain on Saturday left a record 4.22 inches (10.7 cm) in Central Park. LaGuardia Airport got just over four inches (10.1 cm) of rain and Gillette, New Jersey, got 8.63 inches (21.9 cm) in one day, the National Weather Service said.
The vicious storm brought dangerous flooding, washed out roads, closed major bridges and ripped trees from their roots.
Nearly 400 people in the area spent the night at 20 evacuation centers, said Heather Ringwalt, a spokeswoman for the Red Cross.

The torrential rains were a nightmare for motorists as cars, stalled because of the high waters, made it difficult to travel across the city. During the day, visibility on some roads was reduced to zero.

Contributing to the grim traffic problem was the closure for at least several hours on Saturday of the Triborough Bridge that links the boroughs of Manhattan, the Bronx and Queens, as well as sections of the Long Island Expressway, New Jersey's Garden State Parkway and other major roads because of heavy flooding.

The rains also forced baseball officials to cancel the first game of the World Series scheduled to take place in New York on Saturday. The rescheduled start of baseball's championship could again fall victim to rain on Sunday, forecasters said.
LaGuardia Airport was scheduled to remain closed until noon on Sunday as a result of a Delta Air Lines jet skidding off the runway just short of Flushing Bay on Saturday afternoon.
